title: VPC watchdog: fault injection harness and automated fix library for common private health failures
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Goal: ship a deterministic, auditable runbook + automation library that covers the top 8 Private (VPC) healthcheck failure modes and provides both human playbooks and one-click/automatic remediation actions. This ticket delivers: 1) a fault-injection harness (vpc-watchdog-sim) that can reproduce failures in a non-production sandbox; 2) a library of idempotent remediation recipes (shell + terraform plan/apply templates + controller actions); 3) annotated runbooks for PagerDuty and on-call; 4) tests that validate remediation success and rollback safety.

Scope: cover failure modes seen in recent incidents and SLO violations: control-plane API timeout, agent-heartbeat loss, disk pressure on private nodes, kernel/driver mismatches on GPU workers, network MTU mismatch causing model download failures, KV cache corruption leading to late tokens, and Terraform drift that leaves security groups restrictive.

Success criteria (MUST):
- Fault-injector can reproduce each failure in a sandbox within 15 minutes.
- Automated fix for each failure reduces mean time to recover (MTTR) on CI runs by >= 50%.
- All remediation actions are logged with run IDs and can be reverted with a single command.
- Runbooks are tested in tabletop exercise with SRE/PG/PM and validated for clarity.

Remediation approach (high-level):
- Detection: extend the existing VPC healthcheck collector with a \"failure_score\" vector and metadata tags (failure_mode, node_id, last_heartbeat, terraform_state_hash). Triggers: failure_score >= 3 for 2 consecutive polls -> auto remediation candidate.
- Safe mode: automated remediation runs in two-step mode by default: (a) non-destructive checks + light fixes (restart agent service, refresh certs, clear KV prefix), (b) destructive fixes require explicit opt-in or runbook approval (recreate node, terraform taint-and-apply).
- Remediation library: each recipe contains: detection query (promql), pre-checks, remediation commands, post-checks, metrics to monitor, revert steps, and safety gates. Recipes are authored as annotated bash scripts + terraform modules under repo private-ops/remediations.

Runbook excerpts (concise):
1) Agent heartbeat missing (most common)
   - Symptoms: node present in control-plane but heartbeats absent > 90s; failure_score=3.
   - Immediate checks: ssh to node (jump), journalctl -u redwood-agent -n 200, docker ps / containerd ps, disk usage df -h.
   - Auto-fix (non-destructive): systemctl restart redwood-agent && sleep 10 && check-heartbeat.sh --node {{node_id}}. If heartbeat returns -> mark incident resolved and run postmortem autosummarize.
   - Escalation: if restart fails or crashloop observed -> trigger controller to cordon node, drain workloads (graceful), and schedule Terraform recreate with taint tag.

2) Disk pressure / inode exhaustion
   - Symptoms: node shows root or /var full > 90% or inodes exhausted; kubelet eviction warnings.
   - Auto-fix (non-destructive): run logrotate, rotate-redwood-logs.sh, clean /tmp/redwood-cache (bounded), restart kubelet.
   - Destructive fallback: attach ephemeral volume and migrate critical pods, or replace node via terraform-ops apply.

3) Network MTU mismatch (model downloads failing intermittently)
   - Symptoms: S3/model fetch timeouts, retransmits high, MTU mismatch warnings in dmesg.
   - Auto-fix: push mtu-cfg via cloud-init SSM and restart network; post-check fetch small artifact. If fails, route traffic to healthy AZ or fallback model variant.

4) GPU driver mismatch / cudnn mismatch
   - Symptoms: worker reports driver incompatible errors when loading CUDA kernels; model init failures.
   - Remediation: attempt safe driver reload (modprobe + restart gpu daemon). If still failing, mark GPU node for recreate with correct AMI/image; failover to CPU or smaller GPU pool.

5) KV cache corruption (hot prefix causing token regressions)
   - Symptoms: unusual token latency spikes, partial outputs, repeated soft failures.
   - Remediation: allocate cold replica, replay last-good-prefix snapshot (from object store), invalidate suspect KV keys, warm-up prefetch for top 10 prefixes. Post-check: run synthetic request set.

6) Terraform drift: security groups too tight after helper script
   - Symptoms: terraform plan shows unexpected diffs; control-plane cannot reach private nodes on healthcheck port.
   - Remediation: run terraform plan --target=module.vpc_probe && terraform apply -auto-approve in sandbox; if plan includes resource replacements, gate with human approval. Add a pre-apply validation step that runs healthcheck probe against target nodes.

Automation design notes: 
- Orchestration: use the redwood-ops-controller (k8s operator) to run remediation recipes as ephemeral Jobs with annotated run_id and signature. Jobs run with limited scope and AWS/IAM short-lived creds injected by Vault.
- Observability: every remediation emits structured events to logging (JSON) and marks the alert with remediation.run_id and remediation.mode (auto/manual). Dashboards show success rate, time to first fix, and rollback rate.
- Safety gates: destructive remediation requires a 2-step approval by default; integration with PagerDuty response flow and Slack confirmations (react with :white_check_mark:).

Test plan:
- Unit: linter + shellcheck on recipes, terraform plan checks.
- Integration: run fault-injector scenarios in a sandbox account (10 runs per failure mode), assert that automated fixes pass post-checks within 12 minutes.
- Tabletop: runbook walkthrough with SRE, PM, Design on 2025-02-28.

- Private repo with recipes: git@github.com:redwood/private-ops.git (branch: ENG-57311/fix-library)

Open questions / trade-offs:
- What thresholds make a remediation candidate vs a noisy alert? We propose tuning failure_score to require multiple signals (heartbeat + traceroute + kube-probe).
- Should we allow automatic Terraform apply for node replacement? Proposal: allow in Dedicated sandbox tiers; require manual for prod until 3 successful CI runs.
